tutorials.title: Run your own local LLM
tutorials.summary: Install a model on your laptop and compare it to a paid API. No GPU farm required.

steps.title: Pick a runner
steps.body: Install Ollama (terminal) or LM Studio (a friendly GUI). Both are free and download models for you. On 16GB RAM, stick to 7-8B models.

steps.title: Pull a model
steps.body: In Ollama, one command downloads and runs a model. In LM Studio, search a model and click download. Qwen2.5 7B and Llama 3.1 8B are strong all-rounders for code and chat.

steps.title: Talk to it
steps.body: Ask it the same prompt you'd send to a paid API. Notice the speed on your hardware and where quality drops off (long context, niche knowledge).

steps.title: Compare honestly
steps.body: Run one real task (refactor a function, summarise a doc) on local vs a paid model. Local wins on cost and privacy; paid wins on hard reasoning. Pick per task, not per religion.

tutorials.title: Build your first AI agent
tutorials.summary: Go from a single prompt to a loop that uses tools and finishes a real task.

steps.title: Understand the loop
steps.body: An agent is a model in a loop: it reads a goal, decides on an action (often calling a tool), runs it, reads the result, and repeats until done. That's the whole trick.

steps.title: Give it tools
steps.body: Start with one or two tools the model can call (a web search, a file reader, a calculator). Describe each tool clearly. The model picks when to use them.

steps.title: Add a stop condition
steps.body: Decide when the agent is finished (goal met, or a step budget reached). Without a stop condition agents loop forever or wander.

steps.title: Watch it work
steps.body: Log every step: the action, the tool result, the next decision. Most agent bugs are obvious once you can see the trace.

tutorials.title: Ship a web app with Claude Code
tutorials.summary: From idea to a deployed app, using an AI agent in your terminal as the pair programmer.

steps.title: Scaffold
steps.body: Pick a stack you can deploy easily (Next.js or Vite + a serverless backend). Ask the agent to set it up and run it, then confirm it builds before adding features.

steps.title: Work in small steps
steps.body: Ask for one feature at a time, build after each, and read the diff. Small steps keep the agent on track and make bugs easy to spot.

steps.title: Verify before you trust
steps.body: Have the agent test what it built (run it, hit the endpoints) instead of assuming. A second pass catches the silent breakages.

steps.title: Deploy
steps.body: Push to Vercel (static or serverless) or a small VPS with systemd. Add your env keys, redeploy, and share the link.

tutorials.title: Prompting that actually works
tutorials.summary: Practical habits that get better output from any model, with no jargon.

steps.title: Say what good looks like
steps.body: Show one example of the output you want. One concrete example beats three paragraphs of description.

steps.title: Give the role and the constraints
steps.body: Who is it (a senior reviewer, a copy editor), what must it avoid, what format do you want back. Constraints reduce rambling.

steps.title: Let it think before answering
steps.body: For hard tasks, ask it to reason step by step or draft then critique. For simple tasks, ask for the answer directly to save time and tokens.

steps.title: Iterate on the prompt, not the output
steps.body: When the answer is wrong, fix the instruction that caused it rather than hand-editing the result. The fixed prompt pays off every next time.
